title: Why Happiness Never Stays
desc: The new thing feels wonderful, and then, a few weeks later, you barely notice it. In this calm, sourced deep dive we follow one imagined person, Nora, and the sea view she stopped seeing, and go myth versus science, point by point, through why happiness never stays: the hedonic treadmill and what later research corrected, why the brain adapts at all, why we are so bad at predicting what will make us happy, how much of happiness is in your genes, why final choices feel better than open ones, why frequent small joys beat rare big ones, how endings shape memories, why breaks and absence make good things new again, what gratitude and savouring really do, why other people matter so much, and why chasing happiness can backfire. Every claim comes from named studies, with the doubts left in. This video is for curiosity, not therapy or medical advice. The second half is a slow guided wind-down, so you can let the day go and drift off to sleep.
plan: b01: hook. Nora (an imagined person, say so) moves into a small top-floor flat with a big window over the sea, the view she dreamed about for years. Night one she sits on the floor among boxes, just looking; six weeks later she walks past the window with her phone and doesn't notice it. 'Tonight, we'll explore' list (no numbers). Idea to hold: fading is not a fault, it is a feature. Open loop: is there a way to make good things keep glowing? (paid off in b12). Format note: tonight is myth versus science, point by point; second half is a slow wind-down.

b02: the idea of the hedonic treadmill: Helson's adaptation-level theory (1964 book Adaptation-Level Theory); Brickman & Campbell 1971 'Hedonic relativism and planning the good society' coined the treadmill. MYTH 1: 'after any big life change we always drift fully back'. SCIENCE: Lucas, Clark, Georgellis & Diener 2003 JPSP (German panel, marriage: a boost around the wedding, on average back near baseline within about two years, big individual differences); Lucas 2007 Current Directions: adaptation to some events like serious disability is often incomplete; Diener, Lucas & Scollon 2006 American Psychologist 'Beyond the hedonic treadmill' five revisions (set points are mostly positive, not neutral; people differ; one person has several set points; set points can change; individual differences in adaptation). Nora's view fades but she is not 'back to zero'. NO lottery study (owner: no money content).

b03: why the brain adapts at all: sensory adaptation (you stop smelling your own home, stop feeling your watch); Schultz, Dayan & Montague 1997 Science: dopamine neurons in monkeys fire for an unexpected reward, then for the cue, and dip when an expected reward is missing (prediction error), say it plainly without new numbers; Frederick & Loewenstein 1999 'Hedonic adaptation' chapter in Well-Being: The Foundations of Hedonic Psychology: adaptation frees attention for what is new and protects us from being flattened by bad events. Nora's brain has filed the sea under 'expected'.

b04: MYTH 2: 'we know what will make us happy'. SCIENCE: affective forecasting and the impact bias (Wilson & Gilbert 2003/2005 reviews); Gilbert, Pinel, Wilson, Blumberg & Wheatley 1998 JPSP immune neglect (assistant professors predicted being unhappy for years if denied tenure; those denied were not as unhappy as predicted; plus a romantic break-up item, keep wording neutral); Wilson, Wheatley, Meyers, Gilbert & Axsom 2000 JPSP focalism (football fans overpredicted how long a game result would affect them; a diary of the rest of the day shrank the forecast); Dunn, Wilson & Gilbert 2003 PSPB Harvard first-year students predicting happiness in assigned houses: location mattered far less than predicted, social life mattered more (say 'assigned by lottery' is ok only as housing draw; better: 'randomly assigned'). Nora predicted the view would make every morning golden.

b05: MYTH 3: 'happiness is fixed in your genes'. SCIENCE: Lykken & Tellegen 1996 Psychological Science (Minnesota twins, the famous line that trying to be happier may be as futile as trying to be taller, which Lykken later softened in his 1999 book Happiness); Bartels 2015 Behavior Genetics meta-analysis: heritability of well-being roughly a third (about 36 percent; say 'around a third'); heritability is a population statistic, not a personal ceiling; Lyubomirsky, Sheldon & Schkade 2005 Review of General Psychology '50/10/40 pie' and the critique by Brown & Rohrer 2019 Journal of Happiness Studies ('Easy as (happiness) pie?') - the 40 percent slice does not hold up, but change is still possible. Nora's grandmother who always seemed cheerful.

b06: MYTH 4: 'keeping your options open makes you happier'. SCIENCE: Gilbert & Ebert 2002 JPSP (Harvard photography course: students printed two photos, kept one; those who could swap within days liked their photo less, yet most people preferred the swappable option); the psychological immune system (Gilbert et al. 1998) works best when a choice is final; why Nora stopped scrolling other flats once the lease was signed (no money talk, just 'once she had moved in'). Also Iyengar & Lepper 2000 is NOT used (already covered with caveat in lf32).

b07: MYTH 5: 'the happiest life has the most intense highs'. SCIENCE: Diener, Sandvik & Pavot 1991 (in Subjective Well-Being, eds Strack, Argyle & Schwarz): frequency of positive feelings predicts well-being better than intensity; intense highs make ordinary days look grey by contrast (Parducci's range-frequency idea, 1995 book Happiness, Pleasure, and Judgment, mention lightly or skip if unsure). Then memory of happiness: peak-end rule, Kahneman, Fredrickson, Schreiber & Redelmeier 1993 Psychological Science cold-hand study (60 s at 14 C vs 60 s plus 30 s slightly warmer; most chose to repeat the longer one) and Redelmeier & Kahneman 1996 Pain colonoscopy; Diener, Wirtz & Oishi 2001 Psychological Science 'James Dean effect'. Nora remembers a holiday by its last evening.

b08: MYTH 6: 'interruptions spoil good things'. SCIENCE: Nelson & Meyvis 2008 Journal of Marketing Research 'Interrupted consumption' (massages with a short break, TV programmes with breaks: enjoyed more, though people predicted the opposite) - present as a TV/massage experience study, no marketing angle; Quoidbach & Dunn 2013 Social Psychological and Personality Science 'Give it up': students who gave up chocolate for a week savoured it more than those who ate it freely; Wilson, Centerbar, Kermer & Gilbert 2005 JPSP pleasures of uncertainty (an unexplained small kindness kept good mood longer; keep detail minimal, no money). Nora tries a week of curtains closed in the morning.

b09: MYTH 7: 'gratitude is just a greeting-card cliche'. SCIENCE: Emmons & McCullough 2003 JPSP counting blessings (weekly lists over ten weeks: felt better about their lives, more optimistic, reported more exercise); Seligman, Steen, Park & Peterson 2005 American Psychologist (three good things each night for one week: effects lasted up to six months; the gratitude visit gave a big boost that faded after about a month); honest caveat: later meta-analyses find modest effects (Davis et al. 2016 Journal of Counseling Psychology). Nora writes three small things each night, the sea is one of them again.

b10: MYTH 8: 'happiness lives in the future or the past, a free mind is a happy one'. SCIENCE: Killingsworth & Gilbert 2010 Science (iPhone sampling of about 2,250 adults, minds wandered 46.9 percent of the time, people were less happy when wandering, even to pleasant topics on average they were no happier); savoring: Bryant & Veroff 2007 book Savoring: A New Model of Positive Experience; Bryant 2003 Savoring Beliefs Inventory (mention lightly); Jose, Lim & Bryant 2012 Journal of Positive Psychology (savoring strengthens the link between good events and mood) only if confident, else skip. Nora stands at the window for one full slow minute. NOTE: no Short from Killingsworth (channel already has one).

b11: MYTH 9: 'happiness is a private, inner project'. SCIENCE: Diener & Seligman 2002 Psychological Science 'Very happy people' (top 10 percent of about 222 students all had strong social relationships; necessary, not sufficient); Epley & Schroeder 2014 JEP: General 'Mistakenly seeking solitude' (Chicago commuters told to talk to a stranger had a more pleasant ride, while predicting the opposite); Sandstrom & Dunn 2014 PSPB weak ties (more interactions with acquaintances, happier days); a friend visits Nora and gasps at the view, and Nora sees it fresh through her eyes. Check the channel has no Short on Epley trains before proposing one.

b12: MYTH 10: 'the harder you chase happiness, the more you catch'. SCIENCE: Mauss, Tamir, Anderson & Savino 2011 Emotion (valuing happiness highly linked with lower well-being; inducing the value made a happy film feel less happy); Ferguson & Sheldon 2013 Journal of Positive Psychology (trying to feel happier while listening to Copland raised mood) - mixed picture, say so; PAYOFF of the b01 loop: Sheldon & Lyubomirsky 2012 PSPB hedonic adaptation prevention model (good changes keep giving when they keep bringing variety, surprise and appreciation, and when wanting more does not run ahead); gentle research-based takeaways recap list; a year later, Nora's happiness with the view is quieter but steadier; this is curiosity not therapy; turn toward the wind-down.
b13: wind-down 1: evening light, a room settling, letting the day's wanting go; noticing ordinary things as if for the first time (sensory adaptation reversed, no numbers).
b14: wind-down 2: slow breathing, longer out-breaths; three small good things from today, gently, without effort.
b15: wind-down 3: imagined window over a calm sea at night (callback to Nora), waves arriving and leaving like feelings; nothing needs to last.
b16: wind-down 4: body scan from forehead to feet, warmth, heaviness; savouring the bed, the blanket, the quiet.
b17: wind-down 5: last callbacks (Nora asleep, the sea still there in the morning, ready to be seen fresh), thank you, @end teasing the next video 'Why We Get Angry' (anger is next in the queue).
